Data Centers in Space: Hype, Physics and the $100-per-Kilogram Question

In 2026 SpaceX asked to launch a million computing satellites, Google put its first AI chips into orbit and a Seattle startup became a unicorn on the idea. This guide explains why orbit suddenly looks attractive for AI, what has actually flown, what physics makes it hard, and the one number that decides whether it ever beats a data center on the ground.

FL
FrontierAGI Team
October 23, 2026 · 28 min read
⚠️ How this was researched Everything here comes from web searches run up to 23 October 2026. Company plans come from announcements, regulatory filings and press coverage; technical claims come from arXiv preprints (mostly their abstracts), consultancy reports and trade press. Very little has been independently verified in orbit, and many numbers (launch prices above all) differ widely between sources. The calculator, the workload chart and the scenarios are this site's own simplified analysis. See Reading the numbers for the conflicts.

Why anyone wants to put data centers in orbit

AI's limiting resource is no longer just chips. It is electricity, cooling water, land and the years it takes to connect a new site to the grid. Big AI campuses now draw hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts, and in many places local opposition, grid queues and water rights decide where they can go. In June 2026 CNBC summed up the mood: no one wants AI data centers on Earth, so do they make sense in space?

Orbit offers what the ground is short of. In the right orbit the Sun almost never sets, so solar panels work nearly all the time without batteries for the night. Nobody lives next door. There is no grid queue and no water bill. The catches are that everything must be launched at thousands of dollars per kilogram, heat can only leave by radiating it away, chips are bombarded by radiation, and nothing can be repaired.

What changed in 2025 and 2026 is that this went from conference slides to hardware and regulatory filings. The question this article tries to answer is not "is it possible?" (small versions clearly are) but "at what launch price and for which jobs does it beat the ground?"

~$100/kglaunch price at which BCG and Forethought say orbit starts to compete; today's prices are about 10 to 30 times higher

The pitch in one table

Here is how proponents compare a data center on the ground with one in a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, the orbit Google's paper uses, which rides the line between day and night so its panels see the Sun almost continuously.

Earth vs orbit, resource by resource

Green = advantage, red = disadvantage. Qualitative summary of the sources in this article.

ResourceOn EarthIn orbit
EnergyGrid power with long connection queues; solar only works part of the dayNear-continuous sunlight in dawn-dusk orbit, no atmosphere filtering it
CoolingAir or water cooling; large water use in some designsNo air or water at all: heat must be radiated away by large, heavy panels

RepairsTechnicians swap failed parts dailyEffectively none; spares must be launched in advance
RadiationShielded by the atmosphere and magnetic fieldTotal dose and bit flips; memory is the weak point in Google's tests

Six hard problems

The economics: it all comes down to launch price

Every serious analysis lands on the same variable. The chips cost the same in orbit as on the ground; what differs is everything you must launch to power and cool them, and the price of launching it. JPL physicist Slava Turyshev's April 2026 paper estimates about 29.4 kg per kW just for solar arrays, storage and radiators in a 1 MW system, and 34 to 59 kg per kW once the rest of the spacecraft is included. If a ground data center costs $10,000 to $40,000 per kW, that leaves only $250 to $1,000 per kg to cover both launch and building the spacecraft, which he puts at 3.4 to 13.5 times below the current public Falcon 9 price for a dedicated launch.

What different analysts say the launch price must reach

Each bar is the threshold an analysis gives for orbit to compete (lower is harder). The grey bars show reported current prices for comparison. Log scale.

Sources: Google (arXiv 2511.19468), Turyshev (arXiv 2604.27197), BCG, Forethought, Bain; current price estimates vary by source and payload.
  • BCG (2026): a 20-year cost of about $660 to $750 million per MW in orbit versus $230 to $300 million on Earth, a 2.5 to 3 times premium today, narrowing to about 1.5 times over the next decade but unlikely to close.
  • Forethought: competitive with an aggressive terrestrial build-out near $100 per kg, with savings at $50 per kg; about 38% extra non-compute hardware because failed chips cannot be swapped; probably not a meaningful share of compute before 2030, possibly much of the build-out in the 2030s.
  • Bain: at current prices, launch alone would cost more than the computers for a 100 MW system; $50 to $100 per kg is needed.
  • Google: if launch falls below about $200 per kg by the mid-2030s, the launched cost of a satellite's power capacity, spread over its life, could roughly match what US data centers pay for electricity.

Does orbit beat the ground?

Orbit cost per kW = mass per kW × (launch price + spacecraft build cost per kg). Earth cost per kW = your terrestrial benchmark (building, power and cooling over the same lifetime). This site's simplification of Turyshev's framing; ignores financing, links, operations and replacement.

Today roughly $1,400–3,600/kg; targets $100–200/kg
Cost to manufacture the satellite, per kg
Turyshev: 34–59 kg/kW all-in (1 MW case)
Turyshev's benchmark range: $10,000–40,000/kW

What runs well in orbit, and what does not

Not all computing is equal. A July 2026 preprint by Kees van Berkel (arXiv 2607.14172) uses bandwidth models to conclude that inference in low orbit may be feasible, but that training frontier-scale models there is unlikely to compete. Training needs thousands of chips exchanging data constantly at terabits per second with microsecond delays; laser links between satellites today run at roughly 100 to 200 Gbps, and Google's best bench test reached 1.6 Tbps for one pair. Turyshev's paper reaches a similar ranking: the credible early markets are processing data that is already in space and computing built into communications networks.

A scale reality check

The filings are measured in tens of thousands to a million satellites. Musk's projection for SpaceX is that launching a million tonnes a year of compute satellites at about 100 kW per tonne would add roughly 100 GW of AI capacity a year. To see what those numbers mean, compare them with things that exist.

Satellites: what exists versus what has been filed

Log scale. Filed counts are applications, not approvals or plans with dates.

Current Starlink count is approximate (about 10,000 operating satellites is a commonly cited 2026 figure); Three-Body launched count is from May 2025 coverage.
💡 What 100 GW per year would take At the roughly 100 kW per tonne Musk uses, 100 GW is a million tonnes in orbit every year: about 5,000 launches if each Starship carries 200 tonnes, or more than a dozen a day. For comparison, AI data centers on the ground are being built at multi-gigawatt scale per year. Turyshev's 34 to 59 kg per kW implies 17 to 29 kW per tonne, which would need several times more mass for the same power. Both are projections; neither has been demonstrated.

Debris, astronomy and the regulatory fight

The filings have triggered the biggest argument yet over who gets to use low Earth orbit.

  • Astronomers: the American Astronomical Society asked the FCC to deny an "Orbital Compute" application, citing overlap with earlier filings and harm to astronomy. (Coverage differs on whether that application is for 100,000 or a million satellites.)
  • NASA: on about 5 May 2026 NASA objected to Blue Origin's 51,600-satellite Project Sunrise, citing "significant safety and sustainability concerns".
  • Environmental groups: DarkSky International, Environment America and PEER asked the FCC for a programmatic environmental impact statement before licensing any of these constellations, citing rocket emissions, pollutants from re-entering satellites and ozone effects.
  • Debris: critics warn that a million objects in low orbit would sharply raise collision risk, and that automated collision avoidance is only as good as tracking data. This is the critics' framing, not a settled finding.
  • Rivals: Blue Origin called SpaceX's plan "profoundly disproportionate"; SpaceX called Blue Origin's arguments "naive" and "simplistic". One Italian report expects FCC decisions in 2026 to 2027; none had been made in the coverage we found.

Europe's ASCEND study (Thales Alenia Space, 2024) adds an environmental condition of its own: space data centers only beat ground ones on emissions if launchers become about ten times less emitting over their whole lifecycle.

Lessons from data centers in odd places

🌊 Microsoft's Project Natick (under the sea)

A sealed, nitrogen-filled server pod on the seabed off Orkney had one eighth the failure rate of a land control group: 6 of 855 servers failed against 8 of 135 on land. Reporters credited the dry, inert atmosphere and the absence of people jostling equipment. Microsoft still ended the programme ("I'm not building subsea data centers anywhere in the world", one executive said). The lesson for orbit: sealed hardware left alone can be reliable, but reliability alone did not make the economics work.

🌕 Lonestar's Freedom (on the Moon)

An 8 TB solid-state data store rode Intuitive Machines' Athena lander, launched 26 February 2025, which landed on its side in a crater on 6 March and died. Lonestar says the data center was intact, ran during the trip and briefly on the surface, and exchanged data and telemetry with the lander. We found no confirmation that the 8 TB archive was read back. The lesson: the computer is rarely the part that fails; the ride is.

Three scenarios to 2035

🐻 Bear: a niche

Starship pricing stays well above $500/kg, radiators and replacements eat the energy savings, and regulators slow the mega-constellations. Orbital compute stays a niche for processing satellite imagery and defence edge computing. Watch: published Starship prices, FCC decisions, first in-orbit failure rates.

⚖️ Base: inference and space-native data

Launch falls toward $200 to $300/kg by the early 2030s. Orbit carries a growing share of inference and of processing for data already in space, at a premium buyers accept for speed of deployment and no grid queue. Training stays on Earth. This matches BCG's "narrows but does not close" and Turyshev's early-market ranking.

🚀 Bull: much of the 2030s build-out

Fully reusable launch reaches about $100/kg or below, spacecraft mass per kW falls, and laser links scale up. Forethought's case: space could host much of the 2030s compute build-out. Requires thousands of heavy launches a year and regulatory approval of very large constellations.

Reading the numbers: where sources disagree

ClaimWhat the sources say
Today's launch priceEstimates for Falcon 9 range from about $600/kg (Bain) and $1,400–1,800/kg to $3,000–3,600/kg, depending on rideshare vs dedicated launch and the source. One analysis found the only public Starship price works out to about $600/kg.
"$200/kg by the mid-2030s"A learning-curve projection in Google's paper, not an announced price. Others put the needed figure at $100/kg (BCG, Forethought) or $50–100/kg (Bain).
Starcloud trained an AI model in spaceA small nanoGPT model on Shakespeare plus running Gemma, according to the company. A real first, but a demonstration, not a data center.
Google's satellite is in orbitSeveral outlets report the 1 Oct 2026 launch on Transporter-18 and that Google made contact; no performance results had been published by 23 Oct.
Axiom launched data center nodes in January 2026Reported by one blog (11 Jan 2026); Axiom's own April 2025 release announced the plan. Not confirmed from Axiom or Kepler.
Nvidia's Space-1 Vera Rubin moduleAnnounced at GTC in March 2026 with "up to 25 times H100" inference compute; TechCrunch reported none had been produced or shared at the time; no ship date.
"Gigawatt data centers in space within 10 to 20 years"Jeff Bezos' forecast at Italian Tech Week, an opinion.
Radiator area of ~1,200 m² per MWAppears in one source; not verified. IEEE Spectrum's point that degrading coatings require at least 40% extra radiator mass is better sourced.
China's 1,000 POPS constellationThe goal for 2,800 satellites; the first 12 (May 2025) total about 5 POPS. We found no 2026 launches.

🧭 Closing

🎯 The bottom line Data centers in space are no longer science fiction: chips have run AI models in orbit, Google is testing TPUs there now, and the largest launch companies have filed for constellations of tens of thousands to a million satellites. But the physics makes orbit expensive (heavy radiators, radiation, no repairs, thin links), and every independent analysis says it only competes with the ground once launch falls to roughly $100 to $200 per kilogram. Until then the realistic market is processing data that is already in space and edge inference. Watch three things: Starship's real price per kilogram, the first published in-orbit results from Suncatcher and Starcloud-2, and the FCC's decisions on the mega-constellations.
